topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: The development team has submitted a ticket for a web application that is crashing due to high CPU utilization. The network admin has suggested creating a managed instance group to handle the load. Which suggested configuration below could solve the problem?
options: Create a managed instance group with an autoscaling policy based on load balancing serving capacity.
Create a managed instance group with a cluster autoscaler with a fixed minimum and a maximum number of instances.
Create a managed instance group with an autohealing policy that attempts to recreate the crashed instance.
Create a managed instance group with an autoscaling policy based on CPU utilization.
explanation: Option D is correct because the root cause of the crashes is CPU saturation under heavy traffic. Configuring a Managed Instance Group (MIG) with an autoscaling policy based on average CPU utilization automatically adds VM instances when CPU demand rises and scales in when traffic subsides, preventing individual instances from maxing out CPU and crashing.
hint: When web VMs crash under high CPU load, configure a Managed Instance Group (MIG) autoscaling policy driven by target CPU utilization so capacity scales horizontally before instances saturate.

whyWrong.0: Autoscaling based on HTTP load balancing serving capacity measures request rate (RPS) or utilization relative to a fixed max rate rather than directly targeting the CPU bottleneck causing the crashes.
whyWrong.1: Cluster Autoscaler is a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) feature for scaling Kubernetes node pools based on pending Pod resource requests, not a Compute Engine MIG configuration.
whyWrong.2: An autohealing policy only recreates instances after they have already crashed and failed health checks; it does not add horizontal capacity to prevent CPU overload.

question: An application development team believes their current logging tool will not meet their needs for their new cloud-based product. They want a better tool to capture errors and help them analyze their historical log data. You want to help them find a solution that meets their needs. What should you do?
options: Direct them to download and install the Google Stackdriver logging agent.
Send them a list of online resources about logging best practices.
Help them define their requirements and assess viable logging tools.
Help them upgrade their current tool to take advantage of any new features.
explanation: Option C is correct because sound architectural practice begins with discovery: defining concrete logging requirements (ingestion throughput, retention period, query latency, compliance, and alerting) and systematically evaluating candidate tools (including Cloud Logging and third-party options) against those criteria before committing to an implementation.
hint: Always gather functional, performance, and compliance requirements before selecting or benchmarking specific logging or observability tools.

whyWrong.0: Evaluating third-party tools immediately without first establishing clear technical and business requirements leads to unguided tool selection.
whyWrong.1: Load-testing the existing logging tool before understanding what the new application actually requires wastes engineering effort and ignores functional gaps.
whyWrong.3: Mandating a specific product (even a native service like Cloud Logging) without validating it against the team's requirements risks failing critical project constraints.

question: There is one application that has been utilizing a lot of bandwidth by sending out large packets. This particular app attempts to control the TCP window size so that it can maximize its own performance, to the detriment of other services running on the same virtual machine. Which Linux tunable below would you adjust to set the maximum OS send buffer size for all connections?
options: net.core.rmem_max
net.core.wmem_max
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem
explanation: Option B is correct because the application is sending high-bandwidth outbound traffic (large packets) and requires larger socket send buffers. In the Linux kernel, net.core.wmem_max sets the maximum OS send buffer size across all protocols and acts as the hard ceiling for TCP send buffers (net.ipv4.tcp_wmem).
hint: On Linux VMs, net.core.wmem_max defines the global kernel ceiling for socket send buffers and caps any TCP-specific send buffer tuning.

whyWrong.0: net.core.rmem_max controls the maximum receive buffer size for inbound traffic, whereas the bottleneck here is outbound transmission (sending large packets).
whyWrong.2: net.ipv4.tcp_rmem configures TCP receive buffer autotuning (min/default/max) for incoming packets, not outbound send buffers.
whyWrong.3: While net.ipv4.tcp_wmem tunes TCP send buffers, its maximum value is strictly bounded by the global kernel ceiling net.core.wmem_max; raising tcp_wmem without raising net.core.wmem_max will not increase the effective ceiling.

question: A newsfeed web service has the following code running on Google App Engine. During peak load, users report that they can see news articles they have already viewed. What is the most likely cause of this problem?
options: The session variable is local to just a single instance.
The session variable is being overwritten in Cloud Datastore.
The URL of the API needs to be modified to prevent caching.
The HTTP Expires header needs to be set to -1 to stop caching.
explanation: Option A is correct because during peak traffic App Engine automatically spins up additional instances and distributes user requests across them. Storing user session or feed state in a local in-memory variable means subsequent requests routed to a different instance will not see the user's prior state, causing duplicate or stale newsfeed items.
hint: Stateless horizontal scaling on App Engine requires externalizing session state (e.g., Memorystore or Firestore); local in-memory instance variables break when requests hit newly scaled instances.

whyWrong.1: App Engine's request router distributes incoming requests across healthy instances automatically; it does not pin all traffic to a single overloaded instance.
whyWrong.2: Client-side or proxy caching headers affect static HTTP response caching, not server-side session variables maintained in application code.
whyWrong.3: HTTP Cache-Control headers govern browser/CDN caching behavior and cannot fix server-side state stored in local instance memory.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Your company has recently acquired another company operating in Spain to expand your market in Europe. You have to integrate their legacy systems into your company's systems. Your company uses GCP as the primary cloud to manage your applications. Assuming your team is taking this opportunity to modernize parts of the legacy system, what is the best way to integrate this system into your company's systems?
options: Containerize the legacy applications using GKE and run them on the on-prem instances. Use Anthos for managing the applications.
Create a snapshot of the legacy systems and run them on compute instances on GCP.
Containerize the legacy applications using GKE and run the GKE instances on GCP.
Use a Transfer Appliance to securely ship the data from on-prem systems to GCP.
explanation: Option A is correct because acquiring a company with existing on-premises infrastructure requires a phased modernization strategy that avoids disruptive rewrites. Containerizing legacy applications into GKE Enterprise (Anthos) clusters running on-premises allows both organizations to manage workloads through a single unified control plane before or during cloud migration.
hint: Anthos (GKE Enterprise) enables a unified control plane to containerize and manage workloads consistently across on-premises data centers and Google Cloud during phased M&A integrations.

whyWrong.1: Rewriting legacy applications from scratch before integrating infrastructure is slow, expensive, and high-risk during a post-merger integration.
whyWrong.2: A lift-and-shift of VMs without container orchestration fails to modernize the operational model or provide unified multi-environment management.
whyWrong.3: Forcing an immediate big-bang migration to serverless platforms ignores legacy dependencies and introduces excessive operational risk.

question: The Operations Manager asks you for a list of recommended practices that she should consider when migrating a J2EE application to the cloud. Which three practices should you recommend? Choose three.
options: Port the application code to run on Google App Engine.
Integrate Cloud Dataflow into the application to capture real-time metrics.
Instrument the application with a monitoring tool like Stackdriver Debugger.
Select an automation framework to reliably provision the cloud infrastructure.
Deploy a continuous integration tool with automated testing in a staging environment.
Migrate from MySQL to a managed NoSQL database like Google Cloud Datastore or Bigtable.
explanation: Options A, D, and E are correct because migrating enterprise J2EE applications succeeds when teams adopt managed PaaS runtimes where feasible (Option A: App Engine), automate repeatable infrastructure provisioning via Infrastructure as Code (Option D), and enforce quality through CI/CD pipelines with automated tests in staging (Option E).
hint: When migrating enterprise J2EE workloads to Google Cloud, pair PaaS modernization (App Engine) with Infrastructure as Code (IaC) provisioning and automated CI/CD staging pipelines.

whyWrong.1: Cloud Dataflow is a managed Apache Beam batch/stream data processing engine for ETL pipelines, not a tool for collecting application runtime metrics.
whyWrong.2: Stackdriver (Cloud) Debugger is a live code inspection/debugging tool rather than an operational monitoring service (Cloud Monitoring handles metrics/alerting).
whyWrong.5: Enterprise J2EE applications typically rely on ACID relational schemas; forcing a wholesale migration from MySQL to NoSQL (Datastore/Bigtable) requires a costly data-model rewrite rather than moving to managed Cloud SQL.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: A startup in the Decentralized Finance space provides portfolio management services for customers holding digital assets. In order to manage the digital assets, they take custody of their customer's private keys, which are very sensitive and prone to hacking. They plan to use the private keys of high-value assets only when required and store them offline in their on-premise systems. They use GCP as their primary infrastructure and would like to know how to access and update the private keys securely only when required. What is the best way to achieve this? Choose three.
options: Create a VM in a separate VPC and use it to temporarily store the private keys. Create a peering connection with the main VPC to update or access the private keys.
Store the private keys on-premise and copy them to the VM through a Cloud VPN.
Copy the updated private keys back to the on-prem system and delete the VM instance.
Connect the on-prem system to the main VPC through a Cloud VPN.
explanation: Options A, B, and C form the complete defense-in-depth sequence: create an isolated temporary VPC for the external contractor (Option A), establish tightly scoped VPC Network Peering between the temporary VPC and the target VPC with firewall rules allowing SSH only from the bastion host (Option B), and grant the contractor IAM permissions to tunnel SSH via IAP to the bastion host (Option C).
hint: Isolate external contractors in a dedicated bastion VPC with Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding and restricted VPC Peering rather than exposing production VPCs directly.

whyWrong.3: Connecting an external contractor directly to the production VPC via Cloud VPN exposes a much broader network attack surface and violates least-privilege network isolation.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Your company plans to migrate a multi-petabyte data set to the cloud. The data set must be available 24 hours a day. Your business analysts have experience only with a SQL interface. How should you store the data to optimize it for ease of analysis?
options: Load data into Google BigQuery.
Insert data into Google Cloud SQL.
Put flat files into Google Cloud Storage.
Stream data into Google Cloud Datastore.
explanation: Option A is correct because Google BigQuery is specifically engineered for multi-petabyte analytical data warehousing with high durability, 24/7 availability, and serverless ANSI SQL analytics without managing underlying cluster infrastructure.
hint: For multi-petabyte analytical datasets requiring 24/7 availability and SQL query access, BigQuery provides serverless petabyte-scale storage and compute separation.

whyWrong.1: Cloud Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store optimized for low-latency key-value lookups and high-throughput time-series ingestion, not ad-hoc SQL analytics.
whyWrong.2: Cloud SQL is a regional relational OLTP database with storage limits up to 64 TB per instance, incapable of hosting multi-petabyte datasets.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Datastore (Firestore) is a document database designed for transactional web/mobile applications rather than multi-petabyte analytical scans.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: A development team has launched a vital application on a regional managed instance group that must have nearly zero downtime to ensure high availability. You now have to configure a global load balancer to direct HTTP traffic across multiple zones. After configuring the backend, then the frontend of the load balancer, you click "Review and finalize." Assuming you have configured the load balancer correctly, what backend settings do you see upon review?
options: The backend service is web-app-backend. The endpoint protocol is HTTP. The health check is web-app-load-balancer-check. The instance group is loadbalancing-web-app-group.
The backend service is web-app-backend. The endpoint protocol is TCP. The health check is loadbalancing-web-app-group. The instance group is web-app-load-balancer-check.
The backend service is web-app-backend. The endpoint protocol is HTTP. The health check is loadbalancing-web-app-group. The instance group is web-app-load-balancer-check.
The backend service is web-app-backend. The endpoint protocol is TCP. The health check is web-app-load-balancer-check. The instance group is loadbalancing-web-app-group.
explanation: Option A is correct because in Google Cloud load balancing architecture, traffic flows from the forwarding rule/target proxy to a Backend Service configured with an HTTP/HTTPS protocol, monitored by an attached Health Check resource, and backed by an Instance Group containing the VM instances.
hint: An external HTTP(S) Load Balancer architecture links a Backend Service (with HTTP/HTTPS endpoint protocol and a Health Check) to a Managed Instance Group.

whyWrong.1: This option reverses or misassigns resource roles and uses an invalid protocol/component mapping for an HTTP(S) load balancer backend.
whyWrong.2: This configuration assigns the instance group and backend service labels to the wrong architectural components.
whyWrong.3: This option specifies an incompatible backend protocol and scrambles the relationship between the health check and backend service.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Your company has decided to make a major revision of their API in order to create better experiences for their developers. They need to keep the old version of the API available and deployable, while allowing new customers and testers to try out the new API. They want to keep the same SSL and DNS records in place to serve both APIs. What should they do?
options: Configure a new load balancer for the new version of the API.
Reconfigure old clients to use a new endpoint for the new API.
Have the old API forward traffic to the new API based on the path.
Use separate backend pools for each API path behind the load balancer.
explanation: Option D is correct because Google Cloud's Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer URL map supports path-based routing (e.g., routing /v1/* to the legacy backend pool and /v2/* to the new backend pool). This preserves the exact same DNS hostname, anycast IP address, and SSL certificate while allowing independent scaling and deployment of both API versions.
hint: Use URL map path-based routing on a single global HTTP(S) Load Balancer to route /v1 and /v2 API paths to separate backend services while keeping one IP, SSL certificate, and DNS record.

whyWrong.0: Provisioning a separate load balancer requires a new IP address and DNS record, violating the requirement to keep the same DNS and SSL endpoint.
whyWrong.1: Running both API versions on the exact same backend pool couples their deployments and prevents independent scaling and isolated rollouts.
whyWrong.2: A Layer 4 Network Load Balancer operates at TCP/UDP packet level and cannot inspect HTTP URL paths or terminate SSL certificates.

question: When you use Google Cloud Code to integrate Anthos with an IDE, __________ uses your local Docker installation to manage a single Kubernetes cluster on your development machine.
options: OpenShift
OpenStack
Minikube
Skaffold
explanation: Option C is correct because Minikube provisions a lightweight, local single-node Kubernetes cluster on macOS, Linux, or Windows workstations. Google Cloud Code integrates natively with Minikube so developers can build, deploy, and debug Kubernetes applications locally before pushing to GKE.
hint: Minikube runs a single-node local Kubernetes cluster on a developer workstation and integrates directly with Google Cloud Code for local container development and debugging.

whyWrong.0: Docker Compose orchestrates multi-container Docker applications locally but does not run a Kubernetes API server or execute Kubernetes manifests.
whyWrong.1: OpenStack is an open-source cloud infrastructure management platform for data centers, not a local Kubernetes development cluster.
whyWrong.3: Skaffold automates the inner-loop workflow (building, pushing, and deploying artifacts to a cluster) but relies on an existing cluster such as Minikube or GKE rather than creating the cluster itself.

question: You need to reduce the number of unplanned rollbacks of erroneous production deployments in your company's web hosting platform. Improvements to the QA and test processes accomplished an 80% reduction. Which additional two approaches can you take to further reduce the rollbacks? Choose two.
options: Introduce a green-blue deployment model.
Replace the QA environment with canary releases.
Fragment the monolithic platform into microservices.
Reduce the platform's dependency on relational database systems.
Replace the platform's relational database systems with a NoSQL database.
explanation: Options A and C are correct because decomposing a tightly coupled monolith into independently deployable microservices (Option C) shrinks blast radius and change complexity, while blue/green deployments (Option A) allow complete verification of the new version in an identical production environment before switching load balancer traffic.
hint: Reduce release rollback frequency by decoupling monolithic applications into microservices and adopting blue/green deployments for full pre-cutover validation and instant traffic switchover.

whyWrong.1: Removing QA sign-offs or rushing releases into production increases defect escape rates and causes more rollbacks, not fewer.
whyWrong.3: Decreasing automated test coverage or test frequency degrades release quality and directly increases production failures.
whyWrong.4: Replacing relational databases with NoSQL does not address monolithic code coupling or deployment verification, and forces a risky data-layer rewrite.

question: A financial service provider runs their GCP infrastructure in the London region. They promise high service levels to their customers and cannot risk regional unavailability. The Head of IT wants to have a disaster recovery plan for their Cloud SQL instances in case the region fails or becomes unavailable. Regulation requires that they keep the data in the European region. What are the steps for a complete disaster recovery plan that will give them a near-zero Recovery Point Objective? Choose three.
options: Create cross-region read replicas of the SQL instances in Belgium. If failover is required, make the cross-region read replica the primary.
Create a new standby instance in a different zone in Belgium.
Create cross-region read replicas of the SQL instances in South Carolina. If failover is required, make the cross-region read replica the primary.
Create a new cross-region replica in Frankfurt and attach it to the primary instance.
explanation: Options A, B, and D are correct because a complete enterprise DR plan requires automated cross-region replication and firewall/network readiness in primary and secondary regions (Option A), regular failover testing/drills to verify RTO/RPO targets (Option B), and multi-region redundancy across distinct geographic regions (Option D).
hint: A resilient multi-region disaster recovery design combines automated database replication/backups, pre-configured multi-region failover targets, and regular DR failover drills.

whyWrong.2: Relying on manual instance creation or single-zone snapshots during an outage fails strict financial-services RTO requirements.

question: To reduce costs, the Director of Engineering has required all developers to move their development infrastructure resources from on-premises virtual machines to Google Cloud Platform. These resources go through multiple start/stop events during the day and require state to persist. You have been asked to design the process of running a development environment in Google Cloud while providing cost visibility to the finance department. Which two steps should you take? Choose two.
options: Use the --no-auto-delete flag on all persistent disks and stop the VM.
Use the --auto-delete flag on all persistent disks and terminate the VM.
Apply a VM CPU utilization label and include it in the BigQuery billing export.
Use Google BigQuery billing export and labels to associate cost to groups.
Store all state into local SSD, snapshot the persistent disks, and terminate the VM.
Store all state in Google Cloud Storage, snapshot the persistent disks, and terminate the VM.
explanation: Options A and D are correct because VM Instance Schedules automatically stop non-production VMs outside business hours without losing persistent disk state (Option A), while applying department/project labels enables granular cost attribution and budget alerts in Cloud Billing reports (Option D).
hint: Control developer VM cloud spend by applying Instance Schedules to automatically stop/start idle VMs outside working hours and attaching resource labels to track costs per team in Cloud Billing.

whyWrong.1: Deleting and recreating developer VMs every day destroys local persistent state unless complex image export/import pipelines are maintained.
whyWrong.2: Manually exporting machine images daily to Cloud Storage creates unnecessary administrative toil and slow startup times every morning.
whyWrong.4: Writing custom cron scripts on every individual VM to delete itself adds brittle operational overhead compared to native Compute Engine Instance Schedules.
whyWrong.5: Manually moving VM state to Cloud Storage, snapshotting disks, and terminating VMs daily creates excessive operational toil compared to simply stopping VMs with --no-auto-delete persistent disks.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: You have recently migrated data to the Google Cloud Platform and you are ready to connect your on-premise networks to Google Cloud. Review the requirements below and choose the best connection option. The requirements are: Guaranteed network availability and high bandwidth is low. A private network connection is not required. Custom routing is not required. Google Workspace access is required. And the budget to establish the connection is None. Which option fits these requirements best?
options: Direct Peering
Carrier Peering
Dedicated Interconnect
Partner Interconnect
explanation: Option A is correct because Direct Peering exchanges BGP traffic directly between your border router and Google's edge network at a Google PoP for $0 Google fee, providing access to Google Workspace and public Google APIs without requiring private VPC connectivity, custom routing, or a paid Interconnect SLA.
hint: Direct Peering connects on-premises networks directly to Google's edge PoP at zero Google Cloud fee for Google Workspace and public Google APIs when private VPC RFC 1918 routing and SLA are not required.

whyWrong.1: Carrier Peering requires purchasing connectivity through a third-party service provider, violating the zero-budget requirement.
whyWrong.2: Dedicated Interconnect is a paid, high-capacity (10/100 Gbps) private RFC 1918 connection for VPCs, which violates both the zero-budget constraint and the stated lack of need for private VPC connectivity.
whyWrong.3: Partner Interconnect incurs both Google Cloud port charges and service provider fees and is designed for private VPC access.

question: Your company wants to track whether someone is present in a meeting room reserved for a scheduled meeting. There are 1000 meeting rooms across 5 offices on 3 continents. Each room is equipped with a motion sensor that reports its status every second. The data from the motion detector includes only a sensor ID and several different discrete items of information. Analysts will use this data together with information about account owners and office locations. Which database type should you use?
options: Flat file
NoSQL
Relational
Blobstore
explanation: Option B is correct because 1,000 sensors reporting every second generate continuous high-velocity time-series writes across three continents. A wide-column NoSQL database (such as Cloud Bigtable) provides low-latency, linearly scalable write throughput and seamless integration with downstream analytical tools.
hint: High-frequency global IoT sensor telemetry (1,000+ rooms reporting every second) fits a horizontally scalable NoSQL database (such as Cloud Bigtable) optimized for time-series writes.

whyWrong.0: Flat files cannot support real-time concurrent writes from 1,000 distributed sensors or low-latency indexed queries.
whyWrong.2: Traditional relational (OLTP) databases incur row-locking and B-tree index overhead that bottleneck under continuous high-frequency time-series sensor writes.
whyWrong.3: Object/blob storage is designed for immutable unstructured objects (images, archives, backups), not per-second sensor state updates.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: A mobile gaming firm is planning to launch a multiplayer version of their flagship game. They are using Bigtable as a database and an application layer running on GKE containers. Since it is hard to predict the traffic, they are planning to use Ingress for load balancing to dynamically scale the application layer. They want to restrict the traffic from the Web Layer to the Application Layer only and not to the Database layer. What is the easiest way to achieve this?
options: Create a different subnet for each layer. Use VPC Network Peering to allow traffic between the Web Layer and Application layer and the Application and Database Layer.
Create custom tags to identify the GKE containers and create firewall rules using the tags to allow the desired traffic flow.
Create custom tags to identify the GKE containers and set up routes using the tags to allow the desired traffic flow.
Create custom labels to identify the GKE containers and create firewall rules using the labels to allow the desired traffic flow.
explanation: Option B is correct because VPC firewall rules can filter traffic dynamically using source tags and target tags assigned to compute instances/node pools. Assigning distinct network tags to the Web, Application, and Database tiers allows you to permit Web -> Application traffic while explicitly blocking Web -> Database traffic.
hint: In a shared VPC network, enforce tier-to-tier microsegmentation by attaching network tags to GKE node pools/workloads and defining VPC firewall rules matching source and target tags.

whyWrong.0: VPC Network Peering connects separate VPC networks; placing each application tier in a separate peered VPC adds unnecessary complexity and still requires firewall rules.
whyWrong.2: VPC routes determine next-hop packet forwarding paths, not stateful allow/deny access control between tiers.
whyWrong.3: Google Cloud resource labels are metadata key-value pairs used for billing and organization; VPC firewall rules cannot match on labels.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: You set up an autoscaling instance group to serve web traffic for an upcoming launch. After configuring the instance group as a backend service to an HTTP(S) load balancer, you notice that virtual machine (VM) instances are being terminated and re-launched every minute. The instances do not have a public IP address. You have verified the appropriate web response is coming from each instance using the curl command. You want to ensure the backend is configured correctly. What should you do?
options: Ensure that a firewall rule exists to allow source traffic on HTTP/HTTPS to reach the load balancer.
Assign a public IP to each instance and configure a firewall rule to allow the load balancer to reach the instance public IP.
Ensure that a firewall rule exists to allow load balancer health checks to reach the instances in the instance group.
Create a tag on each instance with the name of the load balancer. Configure a firewall rule with the name of the load balancer as the source and the instance tag as the destination.
explanation: Option C is correct because when backend instances lack external IPs and respond properly to local curl tests, repeated termination/recreation every minute indicates MIG autohealing is killing instances due to failed health checks. You must configure an ingress VPC firewall rule permitting Google Cloud health check probe ranges (35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22) to reach the backend instances.
hint: If private VMs behind an HTTP(S) Load Balancer repeatedly terminate and recreate every minute, allow ingress from Google's health check probe IP ranges (35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22).

whyWrong.0: VPC firewall rules apply to VM network interfaces, not to the global front-end IP of the external HTTP(S) Load Balancer.
whyWrong.1: Backend VMs behind a Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer do not require public IP addresses; Google's load balancer proxies traffic over internal VPC networking.
whyWrong.3: Load balancer names are not valid VPC firewall source identifiers; firewall rules must specify the documented Google health check source IP CIDR blocks.

question: Your company hosts many applications on GCP that each store various kinds of data. The Head of Data Compliance is concerned that if there is any PII (Personally Identifiable Information) present in the data, it might attract fines if not processed correctly. He asked you to come up with a solution that identifies the PII, classifies it, and anonymizes it if it has to be processed. He is aware of the dynamic nature of the applications and data, and is looking for a solution that is easy to manage with minimum overhead. As a GCP Cloud Architect, what solution will you propose? Choose two.
options: Use Cloud DLP (Data Loss Prevention) to scan data stored in Cloud Storage, Datastore, and BigQuery, and use Cloud Data Catalog to tag PII data.
Use Cloud Data Catalog to search for the PII in Cloud Storage, Datastore, and BigQuery.
Use Cloud DLP De-identification transformation templates for the datasets that are identified with PII, and Cloud Dataflow to de-identify them.
Use Cloud DLP to de-identify the PII datasets and use them for processing.
explanation: Options A and C are correct because Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP) automatically scans Cloud Storage, Datastore, and BigQuery to discover PII and publishes metadata tags to Data Catalog (Option A), while pairing Cloud DLP de-identification templates with serverless Cloud Dataflow pipelines anonymizes/tokenizes large dynamic datasets at scale with minimal operational overhead (Option C).
hint: Combine Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP) inspection with Data Catalog tagging for automated PII discovery, and execute Cloud DLP transformation templates inside Dataflow pipelines for scalable de-identification.

whyWrong.1: Data Catalog is a metadata management and search service; it cannot inspect raw payload content to detect PII on its own without Cloud DLP.
whyWrong.3: Running standalone Cloud DLP API calls directly without a scalable processing engine like Dataflow does not provide an end-to-end automated pipeline for large dynamic datasets.

question: You write a Python script to connect to Google BigQuery from a Google Compute Engine virtual machine. The script is printing errors that it cannot connect to BigQuery. What should you do to fix the script?
options: Install the latest BigQuery API client library for Python.
Run your script on a new virtual machine with the BigQuery access scope enabled.
Create a new service account with BigQuery access and execute your script with that user.
Install the bq component for gcloud with the command gcloud components install bq.
explanation: Option C is correct because Compute Engine VMs authenticate to Google Cloud APIs using attached Service Accounts and IAM roles. Creating a dedicated Service Account with the required BigQuery IAM roles (e.g., BigQuery Data Viewer / BigQuery Job User) and running the workload under that identity resolves authorization failures following least-privilege best practices.
hint: Google Cloud best practice is to authenticate Compute Engine workloads to BigQuery using a dedicated user-managed Service Account granted least-privilege IAM roles.

whyWrong.0: If the Python BigQuery client library were missing, Python would raise an ImportError/ModuleNotFoundError locally rather than a BigQuery connection/authorization error.
whyWrong.1: Legacy OAuth access scopes on the default Compute Engine service account are discouraged in favor of dedicated user-managed Service Accounts with explicit IAM roles.
whyWrong.3: The bq CLI component is a command-line utility for interactive shell queries and has no effect on a Python script using the BigQuery API.

question: A major department store chain has developed a data pipeline to ingest sales data from both physical stores and their website. The data scientist team recently trained a sales forecast model and deployed it into production. Over time, the model's performance has degraded. As a ML consultant, you need to help design a solution in Google Cloud to address the model performance issue. How would you implement a solution in GCP? (Choose two.)
options: Deploy the model to AI platform and set up a continuous evaluation job to detect model performance issue, then retrain the model
Deploy the model to AI platform and set up a model monitoring job to alert performance issue, then retrain the model
Deploy the model to Vertex AI and set up a continuous evaluation job to alert model performance issue, then retrain the model
Deploy the model to Vertex AI and set up a model monitoring job to alert data skew or data drift issue, then retrain the model
explanation: Options A and D are correct because both describe the fully managed MLOps workflow on Google Cloud: uploading the trained model artifact to Cloud Storage and deploying it as a managed model version/endpoint on AI Platform (Option A) or modern Vertex AI Prediction (Option D) to serve scalable online and batch predictions.
hint: Deploy containerized or custom Python ML models on Vertex AI (or legacy AI Platform) managed prediction endpoints to get autoscaled online/batch predictions without managing infrastructure.

whyWrong.1: Running self-managed Kubernetes clusters or raw Compute Engine VMs for standard model serving adds unnecessary operational overhead compared to Vertex AI Prediction.
whyWrong.2: BigQuery ML is designed for training and serving SQL-based models inside BigQuery rather than hosting arbitrary custom container/framework model artifacts.

question: Your team is about to deploy new infrastructure for a client who has asked you to restrict the team to only the us-central-1 region. How can you fulfill the given requirement for all the projects in the organization?
options: Organization Policy Constraints
Restrict regions in projects
Custom IAM policy
There is no such feature available in Google cloud
explanation: Option A is correct because Organization Policy Service constraints (specifically constraints/gcp.resourceLocations) act as centralized guardrails inherited down the resource hierarchy, strictly preventing users from provisioning compute or storage resources outside approved geographic regions.
hint: Use Organization Policy Service resource location constraints (constraints/gcp.resourceLocations) to enforce data residency and restrict physical resource creation across folders or projects.

whyWrong.1: IAM roles control who can perform actions on resources (authorization), not the physical geographic regions where those resources can be created.
whyWrong.2: Custom IAM roles define granular permission bundles but cannot restrict the region parameter of resource creation API calls.
whyWrong.3: VPC firewall rules control network packet flow between IP addresses/tags and cannot prevent control-plane API calls that create resources in unauthorized regions.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Your company has successfully migrated to the cloud and wants to analyze their data stream to optimize operations. They do not have any existing code for this analysis, so they are exploring all their options. These options include a mix of batch and stream processing, as they are running some hourly jobs and live-processing some data as it comes in. Which technology should they use for this?
options: Google Cloud Dataproc
Google Cloud Dataflow
Google Container Engine with Bigtable
Google Compute Engine with Google BigQuery
explanation: Option B is correct because Cloud Dataflow executes Apache Beam pipelines that handle both unbounded streaming data and bounded historical batch datasets using the exact same business logic, while automatically scaling worker resources up and down.
hint: Google Cloud Dataflow (built on Apache Beam) provides a single unified programming model for both real-time stream processing and historical batch processing.

whyWrong.0: Cloud Dataproc is a managed Hadoop/Spark service best suited for migrating existing on-premises Spark/Hadoop jobs rather than building greenfield unified stream/batch pipelines.
whyWrong.2: BigQuery is an analytical data warehouse for SQL queries, not a streaming/batch ETL pipeline execution engine.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Pub/Sub is an asynchronous messaging ingestion bus that transports events but does not perform stateful batch or stream transformations.

question: You have installed a system update on a group of Google Shielded VMs that have hosted your application for the last three weeks. Before rebooting the VMs, what step should you take to ensure that the VM security features operate correctly?
options: Update the integrity policy baseline
Disable the secure boot feature
Back up the secure memory boot logs
Rotate your encryption and signing keys
explanation: Option A is correct because Shielded VM Integrity Monitoring compares the boot sequence measurements against a stored vTPM baseline. After applying legitimate kernel, driver, or bootloader updates, you must update the integrity policy baseline so the new expected boot measurements are recorded as trusted.
hint: On Shielded VMs with Integrity Monitoring enabled, update the vTPM integrity policy baseline after intentional boot/kernel updates so subsequent reboots pass integrity verification.

whyWrong.1: Disabling vTPM or Secure Boot permanently weakens VM security posture instead of updating the trusted baseline to reflect legitimate OS patches.
whyWrong.2: Recreating the entire VM instance from scratch is unnecessary when a single baseline update records the new boot state.
whyWrong.3: Exporting and re-importing boot disks does not update the vTPM integrity policy baseline and introduces unnecessary downtime.

question: Your customer is receiving reports that their recently updated Google App Engine application is taking approximately 30 seconds to load for some of their users. This behavior was not reported before the update. What strategy should you take?
options: Work with your ISP to diagnose the problem2
Open a support ticket to ask for network capture and flow data to diagnose the problem, then roll back your application
Roll back to an earlier known good release initially, then use Stackdriver Trace and Logging to diagnose the problem in a development/test/staging environment
Roll back to an earlier known good release, then push the release again at a quieter period to investigate. Then use Stackdriver Trace and Logging to diagnose the problem
explanation: Option C is correct because incident response prioritizes restoring service availability first (mitigation before root-cause analysis). Rolling back App Engine traffic to the previous healthy version immediately restores service, after which engineers can safely analyze request traces and logs in dev/staging using Cloud Trace and Cloud Logging.
hint: When a recent App Engine release causes production latency or outages, immediately roll traffic back to the last known good version before debugging in a non-production environment with Cloud Trace and Cloud Logging.

whyWrong.0: Debugging directly in live production while customers experience severe latency prolongs the outage and violates SRE incident management principles.
whyWrong.1: Redeploying untested code changes during an active outage risks compounding the failure instead of restoring a verified working release.
whyWrong.3: Contacting support without first rolling back a known bad deployment leaves customers impacted unnecessarily.

question: What is Google Cloud Armor, and what primary security capabilities does it provide for web applications and APIs hosted on Google Cloud?
options: a DDoS defense service and web application firewall
a permissions management system for Google Cloud resources
an encryption key management service
a service for storing API keys, passwords, certificates, and other sensitive data
explanation: Option A is correct because Google Cloud Armor operates at Google's global network edge alongside Cloud Load Balancing to mitigate volumetric L3/L4/L7 DDoS attacks and enforce WAF security policies (including OWASP Top 10 rules against SQL injection and cross-site scripting).
hint: Google Cloud Armor is Google Cloud's edge DDoS defense service and Web Application Firewall (WAF) protecting applications behind external HTTP(S) Load Balancers.

whyWrong.1: Identity and Access Management (IAM) manages user and service account permissions for Google Cloud resources, not Cloud Armor.
whyWrong.2: Cloud KMS and Certificate Authority Service manage cryptographic keys and TLS certificates, not DDoS/WAF edge filtering.
whyWrong.3: Security Command Center (SCC) provides centralized security posture management and vulnerability/threat visibility across GCP organizations.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: A production database virtual machine on Google Compute Engine has an ext4-formatted persistent disk for data files. The database is about to run out of storage space. How can you remediate the problem with the least amount of downtime?
options: In the Cloud Platform Console, increase the size of the persistent disk and use the resize2fs command in Linux.
Shut down the virtual machine, use the Cloud Platform Console to increase the persistent disk size, then restart the virtual machine
In the Cloud Platform Console, increase the size of the persistent disk and verify the new space is ready to use with the fdisk command in Linux
In the Cloud Platform Console, create a new persistent disk attached to the virtual machine, format and mount it, and configure the database service to move the files to the new disk
In the Cloud Platform Console, create a snapshot of the persistent disk restore the snapshot to a new larger disk, unmount the old disk, mount the new disk and restart the database service
explanation: Option A is correct because Google Compute Engine supports dynamic online Persistent Disk capacity expansion without stopping or detaching the disk. After increasing the disk size via Console or gcloud, running resize2fs inside the Linux OS immediately expands the ext4 filesystem to utilize the newly allocated blocks with zero database downtime.
hint: Persistent Disks can be expanded online in Compute Engine with zero VM downtime, followed by running resize2fs (or xfs_growfs) inside Linux to extend the filesystem.

whyWrong.1: Shutting down the production database VM, creating snapshots, and swapping disks incurs completely unnecessary downtime when Persistent Disks support live online expansion.
whyWrong.2: Provisioning a second disk and rebuilding LVM volumes or copying data offline adds operational risk and downtime compared to online disk resizing.
whyWrong.3: Backing up and restoring the database onto a brand-new VM instance takes hours of downtime for a problem solved in seconds online.
whyWrong.4: Creating a snapshot, restoring to a new disk, unmounting, mounting, and restarting the database service incurs significant production database downtime when online resize + resize2fs requires zero downtime.

question: Your application needs to process credit card transactions. You want the smallest scope of Payment Card Industry (PCI) compliance without compromising the ability to analyze transactional data and trends relating to which payment methods are used. How should you design your architecture?
options: Create a tokenizer service and store only tokenized data
Create separate projects that only process credit card data
Create separate subnetworks and isolate the components that process credit card data
Streamline the audit discovery phase by labeling all of the virtual machines (VMs) that process PCI data
Enable Logging export to Google BigQuery and use ACLs and views to scope the data shared with the auditor
explanation: Option A is correct because PCI DSS audit scope applies to every system that stores, processes, or transmits Primary Account Numbers (PANs). Replacing raw credit card numbers with irreversible or vault-backed tokens at ingestion ensures downstream databases and analytics pipelines only handle tokens, dramatically shrinking the PCI Cardholder Data Environment (CDE).
hint: Minimize PCI DSS compliance scope by isolating cardholder data in a dedicated tokenization service and storing only non-sensitive tokens in downstream analytics and application databases.

whyWrong.1: Encrypting raw credit card numbers inside the main application database still keeps that database and all connected services inside PCI DSS audit scope.
whyWrong.2: Storing full card numbers in BigQuery or Cloud Storage expands PCI DSS compliance scope across your entire analytics infrastructure.
whyWrong.3: Relying solely on IAM permissions without tokenizing cardholder data leaves raw PANs in storage and keeps all data stores in PCI scope.
whyWrong.4: Exporting audit logs to BigQuery helps with audit review but does not reduce the scope of systems storing raw cardholder data (PANs) the way tokenization does.

question: ____ allows you to use a simple YAML configuration file to define how all your containers interact with each other and with external network connections.
options: Config Management
Anthos Service Mesh
Cloud Run
Anthos on bare metal
explanation: Option B is correct because Anthos Service Mesh (Cloud Service Mesh) decouples service-to-service communication policies from application code. Operators apply declarative Kubernetes/Istio YAML resources (such as VirtualService and DestinationRule) to manage traffic routing, mTLS encryption, and telemetry across microservices.
hint: Anthos Service Mesh (built on Istio) uses declarative YAML manifests to configure mutual TLS, traffic splitting, retries, and observability across microservices without code changes.

whyWrong.0: Config Connector manages Google Cloud infrastructure resources (like Cloud SQL or Pub/Sub) via Kubernetes YAML manifests, not service mesh traffic routing.
whyWrong.2: Policy Controller enforces admission-control compliance policies against Kubernetes API requests using OPA Gatekeeper constraints.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Endpoints is an API gateway for external north-south API management rather than a sidecar/proxyless east-west service mesh.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: You have been asked to select the storage system for the click-data of your company's large portfolio of websites. This data is streamed in from a custom website analytics package at a typical rate of 6,000 clicks per minute, with bursts of up to 8,500 clicks per second. It must have been stored for future analysis by your data science and user experience teams. Which storage infrastructure should you choose?
options: Google Cloud SQL
Google Cloud Bigtable
Google Cloud Storage
Google Cloud Datastore
explanation: Option B is correct because ingesting 8,500 click events per second requires a storage engine capable of sustained high-throughput, low-latency writes and wide-column analytical scans. Google Cloud Bigtable scales linearly to millions of writes per second and integrates directly with Dataflow, Dataproc, and BigQuery for downstream analytics.
hint: High-velocity clickstream ingestion (8,500+ writes/sec) destined for large-scale analytics is a textbook workload for Google Cloud Bigtable.

whyWrong.0: Cloud SQL is a regional relational OLTP database that bottlenecks under continuous high-velocity clickstream write ingestion.
whyWrong.2: Cloud Storage is an object store for immutable files and blobs; writing 8,500 individual small objects per second is inefficient and high-latency.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Datastore (Firestore) is a document database designed for transactional web/mobile state rather than extreme write-heavy time-series clickstreams.

question: You are creating a solution to remove backup files older than 90 days from your backup Cloud Storage bucket. You want to optimize ongoing Cloud Storage spend. What should you do?
options: Write a lifecycle management rule in XML and push it to the bucket with gsutil
Write a lifecycle management rule in JSON and push it to the bucket with gsutil
Schedule a cron script using gsutil ls "gs://backups/" to find and remove items older than 90 days
Schedule a Cloud Scheduler job that triggers a Cloud Function to list and delete objects older than 90 days
explanation: Option B is correct because Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management provides native, serverless, zero-maintenance deletion of objects matching a specified age condition (Age: 90 days). Defining the lifecycle JSON configuration and applying it to the bucket with gsutil lifecycle set (or gcloud storage buckets update) requires no cron jobs or compute instances.
hint: Use Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management rules (Delete action with Age condition = 90 days) applied via gsutil/gcloud CLI to purge expired backups automatically with zero compute cost.

whyWrong.0: Running a cron script on a Compute Engine VM to list and delete objects daily wastes compute resources and operational effort for a built-in bucket feature.
whyWrong.2: Changing storage classes transitions objects to colder tiers (Nearline/Coldline/Archive) rather than deleting expired backups older than 90 days.
whyWrong.3: Streaming bucket logs into BigQuery or Dataflow to trigger deletions is overly complex when Object Lifecycle Management handles age-based expiration natively.

question: You have built a three-tier application hosting critical workloads which you are planning to host on the Google Cloud Platform. Due to the low budget, the database is designed as a part of the application server. Your manager has asked you to design the infrastructure in a way that follows the Hot Disaster Recovery Pattern. How would you design the architecture?
options: Deploy one compute engine in one zone, failover to on-premise server.
Deploy two compute engines in two zones each located in different regions.
Deploy two compute engines in two zones each located in the same region.
Deploy two compute engines in two zones each located in the same region but in different projects.
explanation: Option B is correct because a hot disaster recovery pattern demands near-zero RTO even if an entire Google Cloud region suffers an outage. Deploying active Compute Engine instances across two zones in two different regions ensures both zonal high availability within each region and immediate cross-region failover.
hint: A hot disaster recovery architecture requires active compute instances running across multiple zones in at least two distinct geographic regions so regional outages fail over immediately.

whyWrong.0: Deploying instances across two zones within a single region protects against a single zone failure but leaves the application completely vulnerable to a regional outage.
whyWrong.2: Relying on cold snapshots or stopped instances requires manual or slow provisioning during an outage, representing cold/warm DR rather than hot DR.
whyWrong.3: Deploying in a single zone within a single region provides neither zonal high availability nor regional disaster recovery.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Your company is forecasting a sharp increase in the number and size of Apache Spark and Hadoop jobs being run on your local datacenter. You want to utilize the cloud to help you scale this upcoming demand with the least amount of operations work and code change. Which product should you use?
options: Google Cloud Dataflow
Google Cloud Dataproc
Google Compute Engine
Google Kubernetes Engine
explanation: Option B is correct because Google Cloud Dataproc is a fully managed Apache Spark and Hadoop service that runs existing open-source Spark/Hadoop jobs with little or no code modification, while supporting fast cluster creation, ephemeral job clusters, and Autoscaling Policies.
hint: Migrate existing on-premises Apache Spark and Hadoop workloads to Google Cloud Dataproc for managed cluster autoscaling with minimal code changes and low operational overhead.

whyWrong.0: Cloud Dataflow requires rewriting existing Apache Spark and Hadoop jobs into the Apache Beam SDK, violating the requirement for minimal code changes.
whyWrong.2: Managing self-hosted Hadoop/Spark clusters on raw Compute Engine VMs requires heavy operational toil for patching, scaling, and cluster administration.
whyWrong.3: Running Spark on self-managed GKE clusters requires significant containerization and Kubernetes operational expertise compared to turnkey Dataproc.

question: You are migrating your on-premises data center to Google Compute Engine, and need to calculate the number of vCPUs to support your current Intel Xeon CPU processing workload. Your data center has four servers, each with two dual-core CPUs. How many vCPUs would your instances need in total to support the same workload without compromising performance?
explanation: Option C (32 vCPUs) is correct because each on-premises server has 2 dual-core CPUs = 4 physical cores per server. Across 4 servers, that equals 4 × 4 = 16 physical cores. In Google Compute Engine, each physical Intel Xeon core provides 2 hardware hyperthreads, and 1 vCPU corresponds to 1 hyperthread: 16 physical cores × 2 vCPUs/core = 32 vCPUs.
hint: On Google Compute Engine, 1 vCPU equals 1 hardware hyperthread (2 vCPUs per physical core): 4 servers × 2 sockets × 2 cores/socket × 2 threads/core = 32 vCPUs.

whyWrong.0: 8 represents only the total number of physical CPU sockets (4 servers × 2 sockets) and ignores cores per socket and hyperthreading.
whyWrong.1: 16 represents the total number of physical CPU cores (4 servers × 2 sockets × 2 cores) but forgets that 1 physical core equals 2 GCE vCPUs (hyperthreads).
whyWrong.3: 64 double-counts the hyperthreading factor (multiplying 16 cores by 4 instead of 2).

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: The database administration team has asked you to help them improve the performance of their new database server running on Google Compute Engine. The database is for importing and normalizing their performance statistics and is built with MySQL running on Debian Linux. They have an n1-standard-8 virtual machine with 80 GB of SSD persistent disk. What should they change to get better performance from this system?
options: Increase the virtual machine's memory to 64 GB
Create a new virtual machine running PostgreSQL
Dynamically resize the SSD persistent disk to 500 GB
Migrate their performance metrics warehouse to BigQuery
Modify all of their batch jobs to use bulk inserts into the database
explanation: Option C is correct because Persistent Disk read/write IOPS and throughput limits scale directly per gigabyte of allocated disk capacity. An 80 GB SSD Persistent Disk has a relatively low baseline IOPS ceiling that bottlenecks heavy MySQL import and normalization writes; dynamically expanding the SSD disk to 500 GB immediately multiplies available IOPS and throughput online.
hint: In Google Compute Engine, Persistent Disk IOPS and throughput scale linearly with provisioned disk size (GB); resizing a small 80 GB SSD Persistent Disk to 500 GB dramatically boosts disk I/O performance.

whyWrong.0: Adding RAM does not remove the underlying Persistent Disk write IOPS/throughput bottleneck during continuous database import and normalization writes.
whyWrong.1: Switching database engines from MySQL to PostgreSQL requires application/query migration and does not solve the underlying 80 GB disk IOPS ceiling.
whyWrong.3: Re-architecting an operational MySQL normalization database into BigQuery is a major platform migration rather than tuning the GCE database server.
whyWrong.4: Rewriting all batch jobs to use bulk inserts requires extensive code changes across upstream jobs when the primary bottleneck is provisioned disk IOPS.

question: Anthos has a ____ that checks configuration files and enforces their rules against every Kubernetes API request.
options: Config Connector
Policy Controller
Service Mesh
Config Knowledge Base
explanation: Option B is correct because Policy Controller intercepts every create, update, or delete request sent to the Kubernetes API server and evaluates it against declarative constraint policies (built on Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper), blocking non-compliant resources before they are admitted to the cluster.
hint: Anthos Policy Controller acts as a Kubernetes admission controller (built on OPA Gatekeeper) that validates and enforces compliance rules against every Kubernetes API request.

whyWrong.0: Config Connector lets you provision and manage Google Cloud resources (such as Cloud SQL or Storage buckets) using Kubernetes CRDs, not enforce admission policies.
whyWrong.2: Service Mesh manages runtime east-west microservice networking, mTLS encryption, and observability rather than Kubernetes API admission control.
whyWrong.3: Config Knowledge Base is a distractor and not a real Anthos / GKE Enterprise component.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: You want to optimize the performance of an accurate, real-time, weather-charting application. The data comes from 50,000 sensors sending 10 readings a second, in the format of a timestamp and sensor reading. Where should you store the data?
options: Google BigQuery
Google Cloud SQL
Google Cloud Bigtable
Google Cloud Storage
explanation: Option C is correct because 50,000 weather sensors × 10 readings/second generates 500,000 writes per second of compact key-value time-series records. Google Cloud Bigtable is purpose-built for massive sub-10ms time-series ingestion and real-time range scans for live charting applications.
hint: 50,000 sensors sending 10 readings/sec (500,000 writes/sec) of timestamp + value pairs is the archetypal high-throughput time-series workload for Google Cloud Bigtable.

whyWrong.0: BigQuery is optimized for analytical OLAP queries rather than serving low-latency real-time operational charts at 500,000 individual row inserts per second.
whyWrong.1: Cloud SQL is a single-primary relational database that cannot sustain 500,000 transactional writes per second.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Storage stores immutable objects and cannot serve millisecond key-range queries for a real-time weather charting frontend.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Which of the following statements about Google Cloud SQL storage capacity and automatic storage increase configuration are true? (Choose two.)
options: A Cloud SQL database's capacity must be increased manually.
By default, a Cloud SQL database's capacity is increased automatically when the amount of available space is low.
To prevent runaway growth of a Cloud SQL database's size, you can enable the "Automatic storage increase limit".
There is no limit to the size of a Cloud SQL database.
explanation: Options B and C are correct because Cloud SQL enables automatic storage increases by default so production databases do not run out of disk space unexpectedly (Option B), while allowing administrators to configure an explicit 'Automatic storage increase limit' (in GB) to prevent runaway storage growth and unexpected billing spikes (Option C).
hint: Cloud SQL automatically expands storage capacity when free space runs low by default, and supports an optional 'Automatic storage increase limit' to cap maximum disk size and cost.

whyWrong.0: Cloud SQL storage capacity does not require manual intervention; automatic storage increase is enabled by default on Cloud SQL instances.
whyWrong.3: Cloud SQL instances have a maximum storage ceiling (up to 64 TB depending on machine type and engine) and can also be bounded by a user-defined storage limit.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Your company's user-feedback portal comprises a standard LAMP stack replicated across two zones. It is deployed in the us-central-1 region and uses autoscaled managed instance groups on all layers, except the database. Currently, only a small group of select customers have access to the portal. The portal meets a 99.99% availability SLA under these conditions. However next quarter, your company will be making the portal available to all users, including unauthenticated users. You need to develop a resiliency testing strategy to ensure the system maintains the SLA once they introduce additional user load. What should you do?
options: Capture existing users input, and replay captured user load until autoscale is triggered on all layers. At the same time, terminate all resources in one of the zones.
Create synthetic random user input, replay synthetic load until autoscale logic is triggered on at least one layer, and introduce chaos into the system by terminating random resources on both zones.
Expose the new system to a larger group of users, and increase group size each day until autoscale logic is triggered on all layers. At the same time, terminate random resources on both zones.

Capture existing users input, and replay captured user load until resource utilization crosses 80%. Also, derive estimated number of users based on existing user's usage of the app, and deploy enough resources to handle 200% of expected load
explanation: Option B is correct because opening the portal to unauthenticated public users introduces unpredictable traffic patterns and scale. Generating synthetic random user load until autoscaling triggers and injecting chaos by randomly terminating resources across both zones verifies that both horizontal autoscaling and multi-zone failover preserve the 99.99% SLA.
hint: Validate 99.99% SLA resiliency before public launch by combining synthetic load testing (driving autoscaling across tiers) with chaos engineering (randomly terminating instances across both zones).

whyWrong.0: Replaying only existing authenticated user traffic fails to model unauthenticated public traffic patterns, and terminating only a single zone tests zonal failover rather than chaotic multi-zone failures.
whyWrong.2: Using real production users as guinea pigs while randomly terminating production resources risks violating the 99.99% SLA for live customers.
whyWrong.3: Stopping load tests at 80% utilization never validates autoscaling behavior under saturation and includes no fault-injection/chaos testing.

question: ____ is a managed microservices platform that allows you to just build your application into a container, then let Google worry about handling all the infrastructure management from there.
options: Service Mesh
Config Connector
Cloud Build
Cloud Run
explanation: Option D is correct because Google Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless compute platform where developers simply package their microservice code into an OCI container image and deploy it, while Google automatically handles server provisioning, patching, load balancing, and request-driven autoscaling.
hint: Cloud Run is Google Cloud's serverless container platform that runs stateless/stateful containers with automatic scaling to zero and zero cluster infrastructure management.

whyWrong.0: Service Mesh manages network traffic routing, mTLS, and observability between existing services rather than hosting and running containers.
whyWrong.1: Config Connector manages Google Cloud infrastructure resources via Kubernetes YAML manifests.
whyWrong.2: Cloud Build is a serverless CI/CD build service that compiles code and builds container images, not a runtime platform for hosting microservices.

question: One of the developers on your team deployed their application in Google Container Engine with the Docker file below. They report that their application deployments are taking too long. You want to optimize this Docker file for faster deployment times without adversely affecting the app's functionality. Which two actions should you take? Choose two.
options: Remove Python after running pip
Remove dependencies from requirements.txt
Use a slim down base image like Alpine Linux
Use larger machine types for your Google Container Engine node pools
Copy the source after the package dependencies are installed
explanation: Options C and E are correct because Docker caches build layers sequentially: placing COPY instructions for frequently modified application source code near the end of the Dockerfile (after package installation) preserves cached dependency layers (Option E), while switching to a minimal base image like Alpine Linux dramatically reduces image size and attack surface (Option C).
hint: Optimize Docker build speed and image security by starting from minimal base images (like Alpine) and ordering Dockerfile layers from least-frequently changed (dependencies) to most-frequently changed (source code).

whyWrong.0: Running apt-get upgrade in a Dockerfile increases image layer size and can introduce non-deterministic package versions rather than slimming the base image.
whyWrong.1: Splitting every command into separate RUN instructions creates extra intermediate layers and bloats image size instead of consolidating layers.
whyWrong.3: Copying all application source code at the very top of the Dockerfile invalidates Docker layer caching for every subsequent RUN step whenever a single line of code changes.

question: Your company has a lot of distributed applications that need to connect to a database backend. Your chief architect is looking for a way to store and share the credentials of the database securely. She also wants to make sure that there are no unexpected logins and receive alerts on suspicious login activity. What solution would you recommend?
options: Store the variables as environment variables. Check the audit log of the database for suspicious login.
Use Secret Manager to store credentials. Enable audit logging and check the log for any suspicious login.
Use Cloud KMS to store the keys. Check the audit log of the database for suspicious login.
Use Cloud KMS to store the keys. Rotate the keys periodically to avoid any suspicious login.
explanation: Option B is correct because Secret Manager provides encrypted, centrally versioned secret storage with IAM access control, while enabling Cloud Audit Logs and monitoring access logs provides continuous security visibility to detect unauthorized or suspicious credential access across distributed applications.
hint: Centralize application credentials in Secret Manager with IAM least-privilege access and enable Cloud Audit Logs (Data Access logs) to detect anomalous credential access.

whyWrong.0: Storing plaintext or static credentials in Cloud Storage buckets or source repositories lacks secret versioning, rotation hooks, and secret-specific access controls.
whyWrong.2: Embedding credentials directly inside container images or VM environment variables exposes secrets to anyone with image registry or instance metadata read access.
whyWrong.3: Sharing a single static credential file across all distributed applications without Secret Manager or audit logging prevents granular revocation and anomaly detection.

question: Your solution is producing performance bugs in production that you did not see in staging and test environments. You want to adjust your test and deployment procedures to avoid this problem in the future. What should you do?
options: Deploy fewer changes to production
Deploy smaller changes to production
Increase the load on your test and staging environments
Deploy changes to a small subset of users before rolling out to production
explanation: Option D is correct because canary releases expose a new version to a small, controlled subset of real production traffic (e.g., 5-10% of users) while monitoring key latency and error metrics. If production performance bugs surface, blast radius is strictly contained and traffic can be instantly shifted back.
hint: Use canary deployments (routing a small percentage of live production traffic to the new release) to catch real-world performance regressions before full rollout.

whyWrong.0: Deploying directly to 100% of production users exposes the entire customer base to undetected performance regressions.
whyWrong.1: Increasing staging hardware size does not replicate real-world production concurrency, data skew, or traffic diversity.
whyWrong.2: Running unit tests alone cannot uncover distributed production performance bottlenecks that only manifest under real traffic patterns.

question: A small number of API requests to your microservices-based application take a very long time. You know that each request to the API can traverse many services. You want to know which service takes the longest in those cases. What should you do?
options: Set timeouts on your application so that you can fail requests faster
Send custom metrics for each of your requests to Stackdriver Monitoring
Use Stackdriver Monitoring to look for insights that show when your API latencies are high
Instrument your application with Stackdriver Trace in order to break down the request latencies at each microservice
explanation: Option D is correct because intermittent tail latency across a microservices architecture requires distributed request tracing. Cloud Trace propagates trace context headers across every downstream microservice call and renders waterfall latency breakdowns showing exact time spent in each service.
hint: Use Cloud Trace (Stackdriver Trace) distributed tracing to inspect per-microservice span latencies and pinpoint tail-latency bottlenecks across multi-service API calls.

whyWrong.0: Cloud Logging records discrete log entries per service but does not automatically construct end-to-end latency waterfalls across distributed RPC hops.
whyWrong.1: Cloud Monitoring dashboards display aggregate service metrics (like CPU or overall request count) rather than per-request cross-service latency spans.
whyWrong.2: Cloud Debugger inspects code state at a single point in a single service rather than measuring end-to-end distributed request latency.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: A financial data company currently shares data with its clients through desktop software and APIs but is looking to share a particular data set with their clients utilizing GCP. The requirements for sharing this data are as follows: Clients should be able to only read the data and not update or modify any data. Different clients subscribe to different parts of the data and the company doesn't want to share the whole data set to all the clients. How should the company design the offering so that it can share the data set with clients for analysis?
options: Create different data sets for different clients and store them in a bucket. Share each data set as a read-only object with respective clients.
Create a bucket for each client with uniform read access. Share the data sets in respective buckets that belong to the clients.
Load the data set into BigQuery. Create views for different clients and give access to views to respective clients.
Register as a partner on Google Cloud Marketplace and upload the data set as a solution. Redirect clients to access the data set through the marketplace.
explanation: Option C is correct because BigQuery Authorized Views allow you to host a single canonical dataset without duplicating data across SFTP exports or per-client tables, while enforcing SQL row/column filtering so each client can query only their authorized view in real time.
hint: Share multi-tenant financial datasets securely in BigQuery by storing data once and granting each external client access to authorized views filtered to their specific rows.

whyWrong.0: Continuing batch SFTP file transfers fails to modernize data sharing or provide real-time query access.
whyWrong.1: Duplicating the dataset into separate physical BigQuery tables for every client multiplies storage cost and creates ETL synchronization drift.
whyWrong.3: Granting external clients direct IAM read access to the underlying base dataset exposes all clients' confidential financial records.

question: During a high-traffic portion of the day, one of your relational databases crashes, but the replica is never promoted to a master. You want to avoid this in the future. What should you do?
options: Use a different database
Choose larger instances for your database
Create snapshots of your database more regularly
Implement routinely scheduled failovers of your databases
explanation: Option D is correct because an untested HA failover mechanism is a latent single point of failure. Routinely scheduling controlled database failovers verifies that standby replicas stay properly synchronized, configuration drift is caught early, and application connection pools handle failovers gracefully.
hint: Prevent surprise high-availability failover outages by conducting regularly scheduled database failover drills (GameDays) to validate standby readiness and client reconnection logic.

whyWrong.0: Disabling automatic failover forces manual intervention during peak outages and dramatically lengthens Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR).
whyWrong.1: Over-provisioning primary instance CPU/RAM does not test or fix broken failover configuration on the standby replica.
whyWrong.2: Switching from relational databases to flat files or object storage breaks transactional application requirements.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: Your company has decided to build a backup replica of their on-premises user authentication PostgreSQL database on Google Cloud Platform. The database is 4 terabytes and large updates are frequent. Replication requires private address space communication. Which networking approach should you use?
options: Google Cloud Dedicated Interconnect
Google Cloud VPN connected to the data center network
A NAT and TLS translation gateway installed on-premises
A Google Compute Engine instance with a VPN server installed connected to the data center network
explanation: Option A is correct because replicating large on-premises databases continuously to Google Cloud over private IP addresses requires high, deterministic throughput and low latency. Google Cloud Dedicated Interconnect provides direct physical 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps links between your data center and Google's network.
hint: Dedicated Interconnect provides high-bandwidth (10 Gbps / 100 Gbps), private RFC 1918 connectivity with a 99.99% SLA for continuous large-scale database replication.

whyWrong.1: Standard Cloud VPN over the public internet is capped at lower per-tunnel throughput (1.5-3 Gbps) and is subject to internet congestion and jitter.
whyWrong.2: Direct Peering only provides access to public Google IPs (Workspace/APIs) and does not support private RFC 1918 VPC routing.
whyWrong.3: Transfer Appliance is an offline physical hardware shipment box for one-time bulk archival transfers, not live continuous database replication.

question: A global fashion label gets 30% of their revenue from online channels. Their e-commerce website serves customers in multiple geographic regions. They use Cloud CDN to provide a better experience for their users. Their head of e-commerce division thinks that there is an opportunity to reduce the cost of operations of the website. Their CDN costs are a major concern and they are looking for ways to optimize the cost without impacting the user experience. They have asked for your recommendation on how to optimize the CDN costs. Choose two.
options: Enable caching for all the common images and non-personalized content
Enable caching for all the content on the e-commerce site
Optimize images by resizing and formatting them appropriately
Use high resolution images for all the content and use multi-region Cloud Storage to store them
explanation: Options A and C are correct because Cloud CDN costs are driven primarily by total egress gigabytes transferred and origin cache-fill frequency. Optimizing/compressing image and video asset sizes reduces egress bytes per request (Option C), while setting appropriate Cache-Control max-age headers improves cache hit ratios and reduces origin fetches (Option A).
hint: Lower Cloud CDN egress and cache-fill costs by compressing/optimizing static media assets to reduce byte transfer size and tuning Cache-Control TTL headers to maximize cache hit ratios.

whyWrong.1: Disabling Cloud CDN forces every global user request back to origin servers, increasing both origin compute load and inter-continental network egress costs.
